consensus_summary: The blind consensus identifies 'cast into the sea' as complete, final, and irreversible removal or destruction — most prominently divine judgment (the millstone warning; Babylon hurled into the sea in Rev 18:21) — with well-established parallel applications: faith removing impossible obstacles (the mountain/tree sayings), and God's total forgiveness of sins (Micah 7:19). The sea functions as the place of no return. Several responses list, as a common or minority alternative, the overthrow of a kingdom/political power, with the sea symbolizing turbulent peoples or nations.
book_summary: The book defines the symbol as a ruling power irreversibly destroyed and sunk into 'the sea of peoples,' never to rise — especially the fall of Babylon the Great. It applies this single politically-focused meaning across all instances, printing the faith-mountain (Matt 21:21) and sycamine-tree (Luke 17:6) sayings and the Acts 27 shipwreck under the same rubric, and specifies the sea as the mass of peoples/nations rather than a generic abyss.
consensus_core_identification: Total, irreversible destruction, removal, or disappearance — applied variously to divine judgment on the wicked/Babylon, faith removing obstacles, and the burial of forgiven sins.
book_core_identification: The irreversible destruction of a ruling power, sunk into the 'sea of peoples' never to rise, paradigmatically the fall of Babylon the Great.
boundary_disagreement: The book restricts the symbol to the downfall of ruling powers and specifies the sea as 'peoples' (a reading the consensus notes only as a common/minority alternative via Rev 17:15 and the kingdom-mountain motif). In doing so it reclassifies cases the consensus assigns to other frames: Matthew 21:21 and Luke 17:6, which the consensus reads dominantly as faith overcoming impossible obstacles, are folded into the political-overthrow meaning; Acts 27:41 (a shipwreck the consensus treats as historical narrative) is admitted as an instance of the symbol. The book also silently drops the Micah 7:19 forgiveness application and the personal-judgment millstone warning from its core.
material_contradiction: None at the center. The book's 'irreversibly destroyed, never to rise' is the consensus's finality/irreversibility core; 'sunk into the sea of peoples' aligns with a listed consensus alternative (mountain = kingdom, sea = nations) rather than replacing the consensus referent. The reclassification of the faith sayings is a boundary dispute, not a contradiction of the destruction core.
rationale: Both readings agree that the image means violent, final, unrecoverable overthrow, with Rev 18:21 and Jer 51:63-64 as anchor texts. The book keeps that referent but materially tightens it in two ways: (1) it fixes the subject as a 'ruling power' and the sea as 'peoples,' converting a consensus minority/common alternative into the sole meaning; (2) it changes the extension by absorbing the faith-mountain/tree sayings (consensus-dominant obstacle-of-faith reading) and Acts 27 into the political-judgment frame while omitting the forgiveness-of-sins and personal-millstone applications. This is genuine boundary disagreement within the same central category — REFINED, not DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: One could argue for DIVERGENT on the ground that the book reassigns the Matthew 21:21/Luke 17:6 sayings from the consensus-dominant faith-and-prayer meaning to political overthrow, and that 'sea of peoples' is a specific identification the printed citations never establish (no Rev 17:15 or Dan 7 is cited; Ex 15 and Jer 51 involve literal waters). However, because the book's central identification — irreversible destruction of Babylon-like powers — is squarely within the consensus core, the reclassification remains a boundary/extension dispute rather than a replacement of the referent.
